title.value: Assessment of Vocal Cord Function and Voice Disorders

diagnostic_approaches.name: Perceptual Voice Analysis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess voice quality to correlate with laryngoscopic findings as part of the laryngeal exam.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Examiner listens and analyzes voice quality during exam to align auditory findings with laryngoscopy.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Used to break a global descriptor like hoarseness into components (roughness, breathiness, strain, etc.).
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During the physical examination component of the laryngeal exam.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Perceptual voice analysis is a physical examination component of the laryngeal exam.

diagnostic_approaches.name: GRBAS Scale
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Perceptual rating scale for dysphonia components.
criteria_or_scoring: Roughness (R): perceived quality of irregular vibration
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Clinician rates five parameters during perceptual voice analysis.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Higher perceived severity in parameters reflects greater dysphonia elements.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During perceptual voice evaluation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Two common perceptual voice scales are the GRBAS (Grade, Roughness, Breathiness, Asthenia, and Strain) scale

diagnostic_approaches.name: CAPE-V (Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Standardized perceptual rating of voice qualities.
criteria_or_scoring: 10-cm visual analog scale on a standardized reading passage.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Have patient read a standardized passage; clinician rates parameters on a 10-cm visual analog scale.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Greater distance on visual analog scale indicates greater perceived abnormality.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Perceptual voice assessment.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The CAPE-V is a rating scale using parameters of severity, roughness, breathiness, strain, pitch, and loudness, using a 10-cm visual analog scale on a standardized reading passage.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Voice Handicap Index (VHI)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Patient-reported outcome measure for impact of voice disorders.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Patient completes self-questionnaire to quantify voice-related handicap.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Used to track perceived impact over time and before/after interventions.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: At initial visit and follow-up to assess impact and outcomes.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The Voice Handicap Index (VHI) [2] and the Voice Handicap Index-10 (VHI-10) [3] are common patient- reported outcome measurements (see Table 2).

diagnostic_approaches.name: Voice Handicap Index-10 (VHI-10)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Short-form patient-reported outcome measure for voice handicap.
criteria_or_scoring: My voice makes it difficult for people to hear me
People have difficulty understanding me in a noisy room
My voice difficulties restrict personal and social life
I feel left out of conversations because of my voice
My voice problem cause me to lose income
I feel as though I have to strain to produce voice
The clarity of my voice is unpredictable
My voice makes me feel handicapped
People ask, “What’s wrong with your voice?”
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Patient completes the 10-item questionnaire.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Higher responses indicate greater perceived handicap.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Baseline and follow-up assessment of voice-related handicap.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Table 2 Voice handicap index-10 (VHI-10)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Indirect Laryngoscopy (Angulated Mirror Exam)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Office-based visualization of laryngeal structures.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use an angulated dental mirror and headlamp; insert mirror into oropharynx with directed light to view true/false vocal folds, arytenoids, supraglottis.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Direct visualization of structures during phonation and respiration.
limitations: Substantial gag reflex
Large palate
Enlarged base of tongue
Cervical osteophytes
Hypertrophic tonsils
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Most common office-based assessment method.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A substantial gag reflex, a large palate, enlarged base of tongue, cervical osteophytes, and hypertrophic tonsils can prevent examination.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible Transnasal Laryngoscopy (Nasopharyngoscopy)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Visualization of larynx during natural phonatory and vegetative tasks.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Topically anesthetize nasal cavity with lidocaine and decongestant; insert endoscope along floor of nasal cavity to visualize larynx; have patient produce steady /i/ at comfortable, high, and low registers; include standardized reading passage and singing sample.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Direct assessment of structure and function during speech, singing, and vegetative tasks.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Office-based laryngeal examination allowing natural phonatory positioning.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: High-definition imaging with the use of special light filters has also improved the diagnostic sensitivity of the examiner.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Rigid Telescope Laryngoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: High-quality visualization of true vocal folds.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use an angulated rigid telescope (commonly 60°, 70°, or 90°) for transoral visualization of the larynx.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Detailed view of vocal fold structure and vibration (with stroboscopy if used).
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Office-based examination where rigid optics are tolerated.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The degree of angulation is generally 60°, 70°, or 90°.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Manual Palpation of Larynx and Neck
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess laryngeal mobility, elevation, and muscle tension.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Palpate neck and thyroid; observe laryngeal elevation during swallowing; palpate cricothyroid and thyrohyoid spaces during phonation for tension/tenderness.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Normal: several centimeters elevation on swallow; little vertical elevation during comfortable phonation; excessive tension suggests strain/supraglottic recruitment.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Physical examination of the larynx.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: During swallowing, the larynx should elevate several centimeters freely and comfortably.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Inspection of Mucosal Quality (Oral/Nasal/Pharyngeal/Laryngeal)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify mucosal abnormalities contributing to dysphonia.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Inspect mucosa for hydration, dryness, thick mucus, purulence, fungal changes; assess tongue and palate mobility; evaluate nasal mucosa for hypertrophy/allergic changes.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Abnormal mucosa (dryness, thick mucus, purulence, fungal changes) will result in dysphonia.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Routine head and neck examination for voice complaints.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Normal, well-hydrated mucosa is important for good sound production, and the presence of abnormal mucosal surfaces, excessive dryness, thick phlegm/mucus, purulent drainage, and fungal changes will result in dysphonia.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Videostroboscopy (Mucosal Wave Analysis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Mucosal wave analysis of the vocal folds.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Common assessment tool within comprehensive voice evaluation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: mucosal wave analysis via videostroboscopy.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Objective Acoustic Testing / Acoustic Recordings
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Objective assessment of voice characteristics as part of comprehensive evaluation.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Common assessment component within comprehensive voice assessment.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: videostroboscopy, perceptual voice analysis, acoustic recordings, objective acoustic and aerodynamic data, and physical examination.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Aerodynamic Measurements / Testing
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Objective aerodynamic assessment within voice evaluation.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Common assessment tool in comprehensive voice assessment.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: common assessment tools, including objective acoustic and aerodynamic testing, perceptual rating scales, laryngoscopy, and mucosal wave analysis via videostroboscopy.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Videostroboscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Evaluate vocal fold pliability and the larynx’s ability to generate the mucosal wave; document vibratory function to aid diagnosis.
criteria_or_scoring: Magnified view allows diagnosis of mass lesions, scars, adynamic components, loss of tissue
Depth of mucosal/submucosal lesion inferred by impact on mucosal wave
Superficial keratosis/leukoplakia floats; invasive carcinoma sticks to deeper structures
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use stroboscopic unit with microphone (and optionally electroglottograph), camera, and rigid or flexible endoscope. Rigid exam: sniffing position, tongue protrusion and grasping, insert telescope along floor of mouth; phonate steady /i/ at comfortable, high, and low pitches; glissando; brisk nasal sniffs or alternating sniffs with /i/. Topical anesthetic may be used.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Assess mucosal wave to characterize pliability and lesion behavior; superficial lesions float on surface; invasive lesions adhere to deeper structures.
limitations: Method of assessment rather than an objective test
Lack of standardized, reliable methodology
No single universally accepted grading system
Inherent variability in interpretation
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Key examination component for voice evaluation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Videostroboscopy is a powerful tool designed to evaluate the pliability of the vocal fold and the larynx’s ability to generate the mucosal wave.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Electroglottograph (EGG)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Capture frequency of vocal fold closure to aid stroboscopic synchronization; measure electrical resistance across the vocal folds.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use surface electrodes to measure electrical resistance across the vocal folds.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: To aid the stroboscopic unit in determining phonatory frequency.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: An electroglottograph, a device that can measure electrical resistance across the vocal folds using surface electrodes, can also capture the frequency of vocal fold closure to aid the stroboscopic unit.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Glottic closure pattern classification (Hirano and Bless)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Categorize glottic closure patterns during laryngeal motion assessment.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Applied during functional assessment of laryngeal motion and glottic closure pattern on laryngeal exam.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Patterns describe types of glottic closure seen on examination.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During interpretation of the laryngeal examination.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: These include complete, incomplete, hourglass, irregular, posterior gap, anterior gap, and spindle gap.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Supraglottic compression classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify types of supraglottic compression observed on exam.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Describe supraglottic compression pattern during laryngeal examination (rigid or flexible).
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Identifies predominant hyperfunctional compression pattern.
limitations: Compression may be altered between flexible and rigid stroboscopy
tongue extension can alter hyperfunctional state.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Include description during laryngeal exam interpretation.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A common classification system for supraglottic compression divides the types into an open posterior gap-type hyperfunction, predominantly lateral overclosure, predominantly anterior-posterior overclosure, and sphincteric closure.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Mucosal wave properties assessment (videostroboscopy)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess vocal fold pliability and vibratory energy generation.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Record during videostroboscopy at the patient’s comfortable or habitual pitch (fundamental frequency).
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Periodicity reflects regularity of cycles; aperiodicity produces rough signal. Duration of closure is relative time in closed position. Amplitude reflects horizontal excursion/viscoelastic properties.
limitations: Amplitude description is somewhat subjective
Amplitude varies with pitch, frequency, effort, volume
Influenced by endoscope angulation and supraglottic compression
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During videostroboscopic examination.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Mucosal wave properties include phase closure, amplitude and phase symmetry, periodicity, adynamic or nonvibratory segments, and duration of closure.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Videokymography for closed-phase measurement
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Quantitatively measure the length of the closed phase of the mucosal wave.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Measure the length of the closed phase with digital photography or videokymography.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Provides quantitative duration of closure relative to vibratory cycle.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When quantitative assessment of closed phase is desired.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: more quantitatively by measuring the length of the closed phase with digital photography or videokymography.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Acoustic analysis of voice
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Instrumental measures of voice to localize dysfunction within the phonatory mechanism and track therapy progress.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Waveform analysis of digitized sustained vowels and speech; standardized environment; measure intensity and frequency parameters.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Parameters can follow treatment efficacy but do not localize vocal pathology diagnostically.
limitations: Requires rigorously standardized environment and skilled evaluators
Difficult in severe dysphonia/dysarthria; effort dependent
Readings across different equipment/labs not necessarily comparable
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Useful adjuncts for vocal analysis and monitoring progress.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Acoustical analysis and airflow studies are instrumental measures of voice and useful adjuncts for vocal analysis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Phonetogram
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Visual representation of the vocal range (frequency and intensity).
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Measure maximal and minimal intensity at different fundamental frequencies to graph the phonetogram.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Displays frequency and intensity range for an individual.
limitations: Frequency and intensity range are effort-dependent
Values vary with testing environments
Standardization is extremely important
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Characterize vocal range; especially relevant for singers.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Maximal and minimal intensity can be measured at different fundamental frequencies to graph a phonetogram.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Machine learning voice analysis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Disease identification and potential early detection/monitoring via analysis of vocal features.
criteria_or_scoring: Extract features: pitch, volume, tone, duration, intensity
Convert audio to spectrograms or waveforms
Compare to healthy individuals to diagnose disease
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use signal processing to extract acoustic features; ML algorithms analyze patterns using visual representations of audio.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Identifies correlations between sound patterns and throat health; may aid faster, more accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Potentially valuable for early disease detection and monitoring treatment progress.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Machine learning applications have recently emerged as powerful tools for disease identification through voice analysis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Subglottal pressure measurement (direct and indirect)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess subglottal pressure supporting voice for aerodynamic evaluation.
criteria_or_scoring: Minimal subglottic air pressure to support voice: 3–7 cm of water
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Direct: introduce pressure transducer through trachea. Indirect: hold transducer in mouth, purse lips, exhale for transoral pressure.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Provides sample of laryngeal valve function and mucosal wave integrity when combined with other measures.
limitations: Instrumental standardization not fully implemented
Results across equipment/labs not necessarily comparable
Technical expertise required; effort dependent; variability in severe dysphonia
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: As part of aerodynamic measurements of voice.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Normative testing has shown that the minimal subglottic air pressure needed to support voice is between 3 and 7 cm of water.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Airflow rate measurement across the vocal cords
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Quantify average airflow rates as part of aerodynamic voice assessment.
criteria_or_scoring: Average airflow rates between the vocal cords: around 50–200 ml of water
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Contributes to sampling laryngeal valve function and mucosal wave integrity with other aerodynamic measures.
limitations: Instrumental standardization not fully implemented
Effort dependent; variability in severe dysphonia
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: As part of aerodynamic measurements of voice.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Average airflow rates between the vocal cords are around 50–200 ml of water.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Phonation threshold pressure
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Define minimal subglottal pressure needed to initiate vocal fold vibration.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Lower or higher thresholds reflect ease or difficulty of initiating phonation.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Within aerodynamic measurements to assess initiation of vibration.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The phonation threshold is the minimal subglottal pressure needed to initiate vocal fold vibration.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Pulmonary function testing (voice evaluation)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Evaluate weak and asthenic voice and vocal fatigue by assessing ventilatory support.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Poor pulmonary reserve is associated with weak, breathy, poor voice quality.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Helpful for evaluation of weak/asthenic voice and vocal fatigue.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: pulmonary function testing is helpful for the evaluation of weak and asthenic voice and vocal fatigue.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible nasopharyngeal endoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Enable visualization of the larynx in a more natural posture during complex phonatory tasks.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Allows assessment of laryngeal function during complex tasks with natural posture.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When natural posture and complex phonatory tasks are needed for evaluation.

specific_recommendations: Evaluate the larynx for hoarseness of greater than 4-week duration regardless of risk assessment and clinical history.
If there is a risk of malignant or progressive pathology, or if an individual is functionally impaired, assessment should come sooner.
Hoarseness of unclear etiology in a high-risk patient with significant smoking and alcohol history requires expedient evaluation of the voice box.
Vocal complaints by elite vocal professionals such as actors and singers may require immediate management and evaluation at the onset of symptoms.
decision_points_and_pathways: Hoarseness > 4 weeks -> evaluate larynx regardless of risk or history.
Risk of malignant/progressive pathology OR functional impairment -> assess sooner.
Unclear etiology + high-risk (significant smoking and alcohol history) -> expedient voice box evaluation.
Elite vocal professionals at symptom onset -> immediate management and evaluation.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: High-risk patients with significant smoking and alcohol history; elite vocal professionals (actors, singers).
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The American Academy of Otolaryngology in a clinical practice guideline recommended evaluation of the larynx for hoarseness of greater than 4-week duration regardless of risk assessment and clinical history [1].

clinical_guidelines.title: Rigid videostroboscopy performance recommendations
clinical_guidelines.condition: Videostroboscopy for assessment of vocal cord function and voice disorders
specific_recommendations: The patient or practitioner can grasp the tongue in the forward position with a cotton pad or 4 × 4 gauze.
Care should be taken to avoid striking the anterior tonsillar pillars and the posterior pharyngeal wall, as these areas are particularly sensitive.
Patients with significant difficulty may benefit from the application of a topical anesthetic such as cetacaine or lidocaine.
Once the epiglottis or vocal folds are visualized, the patient is instructed to produce a steady /i/ at their most comfortable pitch and volume.
The majority of the interpretation should be carried out at this frequency.
The patient is then instructed to produce a steady /i/ at their upper pitch range and then again at their lowest register.
Additional maneuvers to perform during the evaluation include a pitch glide or glissando.
Brisk nasal inhalation “sniffs” or alternating “sniffs” with /i/ can reveal the range of abduction of the vocal folds.
Recording and archiving the examination is important because stroboscopic interpretation often requires repeated rounds of viewing.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Patients with highly sensitive gag reflexes may have difficulty tolerating this portion of the examination.
alternative_approaches: Videostroboscopy can be performed with a flexible endoscope or rigid telescope.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The patient or practitioner can grasp the tongue in the forward position with a cotton pad or 4 × 4 gauze.

clinical_guidelines.title: Standardization for acoustic voice analysis
specific_recommendations: Standardization is extremely important when eliciting these values.
Acoustic analysis testing in general requires a rigorously standardized testing environment, skilled evaluators, and highly motivated voice users.
Perturbation parameters are not useful for patients with severe dysphonia and dysarthria; however, they can be used to evaluate clinical treatment efficacy.

clinical_guidelines.condition: Vocal hyperfunction / primary muscle tension dysphonia

clinical_guidelines.title: Management options for motion disorders of the larynx
clinical_guidelines.condition: Motion disorders of the larynx (hyperkinetic and hypokinetic)

clinical_guidelines.title: Comprehensive voice evaluation components
specific_recommendations: The comprehensive voice evaluation involves several components including a voice-specific history, perceptual auditory evaluation, visualization of the larynx in motion, stroboscopic evaluation of the mucosal wave, and aerodynamic and acoustical analysis.

clinical_guidelines.title: Multidisciplinary voice care team composition
specific_recommendations: Members of a multidisciplinary voice care team involve laryngologists and speech and language pathologists with voice-specific training and can include other professionals such as vocal coaches, teachers, pedagogues, and medical specialties.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Members of a multidisciplinary voice care team involve laryngologists and speech and language pathologists with voice-specific training

clinical_guidelines.condition: Imaging and visualization of vocal anomalies
specific_recommendations: Image quality is important in evaluating vocal anomalies, and the examiner should choose the best available instruments for evaluating anatomic and functional components of the vocal folds.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Image quality is important in evaluating vocal anomalies, and the examiner should choose the best available instruments for evaluating anatomic and functional components of the vocal folds.

clinical_guidelines.title: Diagnostic prioritization in voice disorders
clinical_guidelines.condition: Overall approach to diagnosis of voice disorders
specific_recommendations: Careful history taking and clinical evaluation are still the most important tools toward diagnosis.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Careful history taking and clinical evaluation are still the most important tools toward diagnosis.

clinical_guidelines.title: Suspicion for lesions outside the striking zone
specific_recommendations: Phonotraumatic lesions typically occur on the middle third of the vocal fold called the striking zone.
Lesions that occur outside of the striking zone need a higher degree of suspicion.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Lesions that occur outside of the striking zone need a higher degree of suspicion.

clinical_guidelines.title: Assessment of Vocal Cord Function and Voice Disorders
specific_recommendations: Include standardized perceptual evaluation tools such as the GRBAS or CAPE-V scales.
Patient-reported outcome measures help to better understand the specific functional effects of voice disorders.
Objective measures like acoustic and aerodynamic testing are useful, but may not fully reflect the patient’s experience.
Direct visualization of the larynx through laryngoscopy and mucosal wave analysis using videostroboscopy remains a key component of comprehensive voice assessment.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: should include standardized perceptual evaluation tools such as the GRBAS or CAPE-V scales. Patient-reported outcome measures help to better understand the specific functional effects of voice disorders.
